pages.title: Our farms
pages.content:
Green Basket started as a market stall run by two neighbours with too many courgettes. Customers kept asking whether we could deliver, so one summer we borrowed a van, and we have not stopped since.

Today we work with twenty-two organic farms, a dairy, a bakery and a beekeeper, all within a hundred miles. We pay growers a fair, fixed price agreed before they plant, so they can farm without guessing, and we pick only what has been ordered, so almost nothing is wasted.

How we do things

  • Certified organic, or in conversion with a named farm.
  • Paper bags and returnable crates, no plastic punnets.
  • Electric vans and one-hour delivery slots.
  • Leftovers go to the community kitchen down the road.

posts.title: What’s in season this autumn
posts.excerpt: Apples, squash, the last tomatoes and the first kale: what our growers are picking right now.
posts.content:
Autumn is the busiest harvest of the year on our farms. The tomato tunnels are giving their last heavy pickings, the orchards are full, and the first frosts are sweetening the kale and the parsnips.

Right now the boxes are full of apples, squash, beetroot, leeks, rainbow carrots and the last of the courgettes. Later in the month the brassicas arrive: kale, sprouts on the stalk and crinkly savoy cabbage.

Cooking tip from our growers: roast everything. A tray of squash, carrots and red onion with oil, salt and a spoon of honey is the easiest dinner of the season.

posts.title: Meet the orchard family
posts.excerpt: Three generations, eleven varieties of apple and a lot of patience.
posts.content:
Our apples come from an orchard that has been farmed by the same family for three generations, and organically for thirty years. The trees are old and wide, and sheep graze the grass underneath them all winter.

They grow eleven varieties, so the apples in your bag change through the season: early, sharp reds in late summer, then sweeter crunchy ones, and finally the russets that keep until spring.

Everything is picked by hand. It is slower, but it means the fruit is not bruised, and it lasts for weeks in a cool place at home.

posts.title: A loaf that takes thirty hours
posts.excerpt: Why our bakers let the dough rest overnight, and why it tastes better for it.
posts.content:
Our sourdough starts the day before you eat it. In the morning the bakers mix flour, water and a starter that is older than the bakery itself, then fold the dough by hand every hour through the afternoon.

In the evening the loaves are shaped and left in a cool room overnight. That long, slow rest is where the flavour comes from, and it makes the bread easier to digest too.

At four in the morning the ovens are hot, the loaves go in, and by seven they are cooling on racks, ready for the vans. Wrap it in a tea towel, keep it cut side down, and it will be good for days.

products.name: Heirloom Tomatoes
products.description:
A mix of old varieties in red, yellow, green-striped and deep purple, grown in unheated polytunnels and picked ripe. Sweet, juicy and wildly different from supermarket tomatoes.

About 500 g. Keep them out of the fridge for the best flavour.
products.short_description: A colourful 500 g mix of old tomato varieties, picked ripe.

reviews.author: Nadia
reviews.content: These taste like summer. The striped green ones are my favourite in a salad with good oil.

products.name: Crisp Apples

Crunchy, sweet-sharp apples from a family orchard that has farmed organically for thirty years. The variety changes through the season, from early reds to late russets.

Choose a 1 kg bag for the week or 2 kg for the lunchbox crowd.
products.short_description: Seasonal orchard apples, sold by the kilo.

reviews.author: Owen
reviews.content: Proper crunch and not waxy at all. The kids eat them faster than I can restock.

A bunch of about 600 g.

200 g.

1 litre.

250 g wedge.

About 800 g.

products.short_description: Chewy brown-butter oat cookies, a bag of eight.

products.name: Wildflower Honey
products.description:
Raw, unfiltered honey from hives kept in meadows and hedgerows. Its flavour changes with the season: light and floral in spring, deeper and darker by late summer.

340 g jar.

500 ml tin.
